item.title: SoftBank posts $7 bn loss as US data centre costs mount amid AI concerns
item.description: The Japanese conglomerate's first net loss in nearly two years follows a reassessment of its US data centre procurement strategy amid concerns over AI investment returns ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Min Jeong Lee SoftBank Group Corp. reported its first net loss in almost two years after swallowing a $3.7 billion writedown over its US data-center projects amid rising fears around the sustainability of AI growth. The Tokyo-based backer of OpenAI tumbled to a 1.12 trillion yen ($7.1 billion) loss in its fiscal second quarter after shouldering non-refundable advance payments related to power generation at projects including an ambitious Ohio data center push. Analysts on average expected a profit of 129 billion yen. After reserving manufacturing capacity for power generation equipment for AI data center projects in the US, the company revised its procurement strategy. That follows a sharp revision in the global AI outlook after the victory of Democratic candidates running on anti-data-center platforms during the US midterm elections. SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son has directed billions of dollars into AI-related hardware and applications, betting on a technology that he’s said will bring huge returns over the long-term. But it’s now fielding fears over the debt it’s taken on to finance its mounting AI bets that include cumulative investments of almost $65 billion in OpenAI and the acquisition of data-center operator DigitalBridge Group Inc. The company had previously hurried to secure power-generation equipment for data centers in advance, Chief Financial Officer Yoshimitsu Goto said during an earnings conference Tuesday. “We’ve decided to conduct a thorough reassessment” including a review of SoftBank’s procurement strategy, he said. “We need to watch closely” the impact of the US midterm elections on AI sentiment, he said.  Declines in the stock prices of chipmakers Arm Holdings Plc and Intel Corp., as well as Korean e-commerce giant Coupang Inc., further dragged down SoftBank’s bottom line. The Vision Fund segment, which oversees stakes in hundreds of tech startups, logged a loss of 81.6 billion yen, compared with market expectations for a profit. SoftBank’s own shares have plunged more than 50 per cent from their record high in June, and volatility in its stock price has been high as investors try to gauge the risks and opportunities around its AI investments.  In the wake of the US midterms, investors were weighing a valuation as low as $1.1 trillion for Anthropic, down from a previously touted figure of $2 trillion, people familiar with the matter said. OpenAI raised about $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, after initially seeking $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion value, Bloomberg News reported. Son’s reliance on debt markets to finance his expanding list of AI investments has also made SoftBank’s bonds especially sensitive and lifting its credit default swaps hit their highest in years. The company’s loan-to-value ratio stood at 15.9 per cent at the end of September, well below the 25 per cent threshold it’s set to ensure financial stability, Goto said.

item.title: Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with faster AI capabilities
item.description: Anthropic says its latest AI models offer faster responses and stronger coding, reasoning and research capabilities, while Fable 5.2 comes with lower pricing and safeguards ...
item.dc:creator: Vrinda Goel
item.content:encoded: Anthropic on Monday announced the launch of its latest and most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. The company says these models offer significant improvements in coding, reasoning and visual tasks, along with clearer communication. The upgraded models can generate outputs up to 30 per cent faster than their predecessors, Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1. Anthropic has also reduced Fable's pricing from $10 to $8 per million input tokens, making Fable 5.2 cheaper than its primary competitor, GPT-6 Astra. What can Anthropic's Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 do? Anthropic said Fable 5.2 can handle more complex software engineering work, hardware-related tasks such as controlling robots, and long-running projects. It is also designed to coordinate more than 1,000 AI agents simultaneously. The company said early testers found that the new models communicate more clearly than previous Fable and Mythos versions. They also showed better judgement on ambiguous, data-heavy research and analysis tasks, particularly those involving abstract reasoning and design. Fable 5.2 can function as an adviser, with smaller models such as Haiku, Sonnet or Opus consulting it to solve difficult problems. It can also act as an orchestrator, delegating simpler tasks to smaller models. Anthropic recommends that users begin with Claude Opus 5.5, which it describes as its strongest everyday model, for most coding and knowledge-based tasks. They can then move to Fable or Mythos for more complex work, or use Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 for less demanding tasks. Mythos 5.2 is being made available to select organisations and is described by Anthropic as its most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. The company says it can identify more vulnerabilities than earlier models and is better at reproducing and fixing them. Fable 5.2, meanwhile, has safeguards that block most cybersecurity-related tasks. Safety testing Anthropic said it conducted extensive pre-release safety testing on the model underlying both releases. The company said high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low and that the model performed as well as, or better than, recent versions on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2's cybersecurity and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1, while producing fewer unnecessary blocks. Anthropic also said it had introduced its strongest protections yet against distillation attacks. Where are Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 available? Claude Fable 5.2 is available across platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. Anthropic is also offering eligible paid subscribers additional usage this week. Subscribers on plans and seats that include Fable models will receive one to three usage resets, depending on how long they have subscribed. Fable will also be included for up to 50 per cent of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Mythos 5.2 through Anthropic's Cyber Verification Programme. Fast mode for both models is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (both Anthropic-managed and Google-managed) and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic-hosted). Access to Mythos 5.2's fast mode is restricted to organisations participating in Anthropic's verification programmes.

item.title: Trump signals end of Iran war, says further airstrikes won't be necessary
item.description: Trump said Iran's military was 'effectively over' but warned that US forces remained 'locked and loaded'. His remarks came after talks with Qatar's PM on efforts to reach a deal and end the conflict ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Jeff Mason President Donald Trump said further strikes on Iran wouldn’t be necessary but the US remains “locked and loaded,” an indication that he’s winding down the conflict after Republicans’ midterm elections loss underscored its deep unpopularity. “Iran, militarily, is effectively over,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday afternoon. “We’re just keeping it the status quo, and we’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbors.” The comments, which build on signs that the US and Iran are moving closer to a breakthrough to end the war, lowered the temperature on the conflict to a point it hadn’t been since the two nations signed a memorandum of understanding in June. The two sides later rejected it and resumed exchanges of strikes. Trump met earlier Monday with Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, whose nation has served as a mediator between Washington and Tehran. In a post on X, Al-Thani thanked Trump and Vice President JD Vance and said he was “grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region.” The tone of Trump’s remarks put him at odds with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who had told reporters on Sunday that he didn’t have any progress to report and the two sides weren’t on the verge of a breakthrough. “Right now it hasn’t been very productive, because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable but, in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic,” Rubio said. Trump, however, didn’t completely rule out further strikes and said American forces remain in the region. The US remains “locked and loaded” in case a new military campaign becomes necessary, he added. The president framed the latest approach largely as a concession to the US allies in the region including the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Saudi Arabia that have come under attack by Iran and its confederates and whose economies have been hit hard by the conflict. Trump began the war against Iran in February with Israel and promised that it would conclude in a matter of weeks. Months later, without a resolution, concerns about the war and the higher fuel prices it generated helped propel Democrats to victory in the Nov. 3 elections, winning majorities from Trump’s Republican Party in the House of Representatives and the Senate. Vance, a possible Republican presidential candidate in 2028, blamed the war for the disastrous GOP defeat. Trump has said he does not regret starting the conflict to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon but acknowledged that it hurt his party politically in the midterms. Any resumption of all-out hostilities between Washington and Tehran would likely push up oil and energy prices, and lead to fresh assaults by the Iran on its neighbors. Iran has previously said the US must end a naval blockade of its Persian Gulf ports and lift sanctions as preconditions for resuming peace talks. The US wants Iran to end attacks ships in the Strait of Hormuz, allow energy flows through the crucial waterway to resume and to offer concessions regarding its nuclear program. The president’s meeting with the Qatari prime minister indicates his interest in the latest negotiations. Trump has promised that fuel prices would come down as soon as the war ended and suggested that would happen after the election, but he has vacillated publicly between suggesting the US would launch fresh attacks against Iran and using more conciliatory language toward Tehran. One official with knowledge of the talks said Rubio’s comments are more to gain leverage than a sign the negotiations are actually breaking down. Overnight, the US again struck Qeshm Island, state-run Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting reported, citing the deputy governor of Hormozgan province. There was no damage to essential infrastructure and the situation is under control, 2 said. That followed similar strikes last week, described by the US as defensive operations. Since a truce in April, the two sides have skirmished regularly but stopped short of a major escalation. Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets Tehran’s demands remains on the table, Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said at a press conference on Monday. “The return of security to the world’s energy arteries requires genuine political will from the other side to break out of the stalemate caused by aggression,” he said.

item.title: US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review
item.description: The United States is set to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the UN's top rights body since it was created two decades ago.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review

US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review Trump administration declines to participate in the UN Human Rights Council's Universal Periodic Review, which examines the rights records of all 193 member states every four to five years

The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago | Image: Bloomberg

AP Geneva 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 10 2026 | 2:47 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The United States is set to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the UN's top rights body since it was created two decades ago. The Trump administration last year pulled the US out of the Human Rights Council, accusing it of an anti-US and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn't uphold the very values it promotes. Supporters back the council's mandate to keep tabs on human rights in all UN member states including the US, which has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific - which the administration has said are designed to protect US workers and help keep the country safe.

The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 UN member states - generally about every four to five years - as part of a process known as the universal periodic review. The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the US government might change its mind. Also Read

It did not. "(W)e give no credibility to the agency," a State Department spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press. "This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own values' as it pushes anti-American rhetoric," the spokesperson said, alleging the council's "persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators."   The council says the process requires participation of the country in question, and in the case of an absence of any national representatives, the review cannot go forward.

As part of such reviews, national delegations - which at times can include a dozen officials or more - make a presentation, face questions and hear recommendations from other national envoys. It's supposed to be a sweeping and constructive process, akin to holding up a mirror to governments to improve their human rights policies. Critics of the US snub warn that the walkout could encourage other countries - many of which bristle about intense scrutiny from human rights monitors - to follow suit. Jamil Dakwar, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's human rights program, said: "The administration is saying to the world, we don't care about whether you would review us or not, we're going to continue to violate human rights unabashed'."   "And we are saying: No, enough is enough. This council should hold the United States accountable'," he told reporters Monday in Geneva, as part of a push by civil society to raise awareness about the US rights record.

He said the ACLU and allies have called on the UN human rights chief to respond by presenting an update on rights in the United States early next year. Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute who was the council's first secretary, said the US walkout could affect the credibility of the council's review system. "If the predominant global power - which has always claimed to adhere to the human rights norms - doesn't show up and doesn't even justify why, then you are in big trouble," he said.
